prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map establishes a tiered indoor layout, showing an open book in the lower foreground within arm's reach at roughly 0.3–0.5 m (bright white), a couch to the left and a cylindrical silver vase on a glass coffee table at about 0.8–1.2 m (medium-bright grey), a standing person on the left at roughly 1.5–2.0 m (about 0.5–1.0 m behind the couch and vase), and a white TV stand with a TV above it and a potted plant to its left at 2.5–3.0 m against the back window wall. In frames 1–4, the standing person's upper body is cropped above the top edge and their lower legs are partly occluded behind the couch armrest, while the book occludes the front edge of the coffee table; in frame 4 the book drops lower and the vase shifts closer and brighter (~0.7 m) as the camera wearer leans forward and tilts up, and in frame 5 the camera pitches sharply upward and right to reveal the person's full upper torso and head facing toward the camera wearer while the book moves completely out of view. This map makes it much easier than the RGB image to judge the continuous metric separation between the dark-clothed person and the dark TV screen or shadowed floor behind them, as well as the exact 3D relief of the couch cushions and cylindrical vase. However, the depth map is unreliable on the reflective glass coffee table surface (which appears as a dark void in frames 1–3 before jumping in brightness in frame 4) and in frame 5 where per-frame normalization shifts the background TV and stand to look nearly as bright and near as the standing person.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map delineates discrete objects across the room, identifying the grey couch on the left (at ~1.0 m, within reach of both the camera wearer and the standing person), the standing person behind it on the left (~1.5–2.0 m away, with their upper body out of view in frames 1–4 and their lower legs occluded by the couch), the silver vase on the table (~1.0–1.2 m away, ~0.5 m right of the couch), a tall potted plant (~2.5 m away, behind the vase) with its pot labelled as a second vase, a small potted plant on the TV stand shelf (~0.5 m right of the tall plant), and the TV above the stand (~2.5–3.0 m away, detected only in frame 4). Across frames 1–4 the camera wearer stays seated near the couch and table before tilting up in frame 5, where the standing person's head and torso come into view facing toward the camera wearer at ~1.8–2.0 m while the foreground couch and silver vase drop out of the lower frame. Compared to the RGB strip, segmentation clearly separates the dark-clothed person's silhouette from the dark background and isolates the overlapping foliage and pot of the background plant behind the silver vase. However, the map shows severe class and instance unreliability: it misses the foreground book and glass coffee table entirely, falsely labels the printed portraits inside the book as three or four tiny 'person' instances at 0.3–0.5 m (and the curved book page as an 'umbrella' in frame 3), mislabels the couch pillow as a 'dog' and the silver vase as a 'chair' in frame 1, misses the foreground silver vase in frame 4, and misclassifies the distant TV and stand as a 'laptop' and 'couch' in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is completely blank in frames 1–2, shows a small cluster of yellow keypoints near the bottom right of frame 3, is blank again in frame 4, and displays a single yellow body skeleton on the left in frame 5 with no magenta hand skeletons detected in any frame. Using the RGB context, the standing person is about 1.5–2.0 m away on the left (within arm's reach of the couch armrest just in front of them, and about 1.0–1.5 m left of the distant TV stand), but because their head and shoulders are cropped out above the frame in frames 1–4 and their legs are partly occluded by the couch, the pose estimator fails to detect them until the camera tilts upward in frame 5. In frame 5, the yellow torso, hip, leg, and head keypoints show the standing person upright and facing roughly toward the camera wearer with their right arm bent near their side, while the foreground book, vase, and couch (previously within 0.3–1.2 m of the camera wearer) fall partly or fully below the field of view. In frame 5, the skeleton makes the person's shoulder alignment, hip orientation, and torso tilt explicitly visible despite the heavy motion blur and dark clothing that obscure body contours in the RGB image. However, the pose map is highly unreliable in frames 1–4 because it completely misses the truncated standing person, fails to track any hands or arms within reach, and hallucinates a spurious body skeleton on the 2D printed photographs inside the foreground book (~0.4 m away) in frame 3.
